chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Barqi, from Sa'd ibn Sa'd, from al-Rida (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him about the meat of barazin (horses/donkeys), horses, and mules. He said: 'Do not eat it.' The meaning in all these narrations is that we should interpret them as indicating a type of dislike (karahah) rather than prohibition (haram), based on the evidence of the earlier narrations, and this adds clarity to that.

key_terms.الْكَرَاهِيَةِ: Dislike (a legal status between permissible and forbidden)
key_terms.لُحُومِ الْبَرَاذِينِ: Meat of barazin (a term often referring to horses or donkeys)

ai.seo_question: Is the meat of horses and mules forbidden or merely disliked in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Imam al-Rida (peace be upon him) clarifies that the meat of barazin (likely donkeys or a specific breed), horses, and mules is not strictly prohibited (haram) but rather disliked (karahat), a nuance derived from reconciling seemingly contradictory narrations. This ruling reflects the Shia scholarly principle of distinguishing between absolute prohibition and recommended avoidance based on the context of the evidence. The text highlights the methodological rigor of the Imams in resolving legal ambiguities through comparative analysis of hadith.
